Definitions

📍 Geography Terms

Latitude
Horizontal lines running east–west around the globe, measuring how far NORTH or SOUTH a place is from the Equator. Measured in degrees (°). Think: LAT = fLAT lines across the map.
👆 Tap to reveal
Longitude
Vertical lines running north–south on a map, measuring how far EAST or WEST a place is from the Prime Meridian. Measured in degrees (°). Think: LONG lines going the LONG way (top to bottom).
👆 Tap to reveal
Equator
The imaginary line at 0° latitude that circles the middle of the Earth, dividing it into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres. The hottest part of Earth! St. Kitts is in the Northern Hemisphere. 🇰🇳
👆 Tap to reveal
Prime Meridian
The imaginary line at 0° longitude running through Greenwich, England. It divides Earth into Eastern and Western Hemispheres. Together with the Equator, it forms the world's coordinate grid.
👆 Tap to reveal
Hemisphere
Half of the Earth. The Equator divides Earth into Northern/Southern Hemispheres. The Prime Meridian divides it into Eastern/Western. St. Kitts is in the Northern AND Western Hemispheres!
👆 Tap to reveal
Absolute Location
The EXACT position of a place on Earth using latitude AND longitude coordinates. Example: St. Kitts = 17.3°N, 62.7°W. Like GPS coordinates — totally precise!
👆 Tap to reveal
Relative Location
Describing WHERE a place is relative to other places using landmarks and directions. Example: "St. Kitts is east of Puerto Rico and north of Nevis." NOT using coordinates.
👆 Tap to reveal
Population Density
The average number of people per square mile or km in an area. High density = crowded (like Tokyo). Low density = spread out (like Mongolia). Calculated by: total people ÷ total area.
👆 Tap to reveal
Tsunami
A giant ocean wave caused by an earthquake or volcanic eruption UNDER the ocean floor. Can travel at 500+ mph! Japan is at constant risk because it sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire.
👆 Tap to reveal
Dynasty
A line of rulers from the SAME FAMILY that holds power for a long time, passing it from parent to child. China had 11 dynasties from the Xia (2200 BC) to the Qing (ended 1911).
👆 Tap to reveal
Endemic
A species (plant or animal) found ONLY in one specific region — nowhere else on Earth. Example: the Komodo dragon is endemic to Indonesia. The one-horned rhino is endemic to South Asia.
👆 Tap to reveal
Plantation
A large farm where ONE single crop is grown on a big scale for EXPORT (selling to other countries). Europeans set up tea, coffee, tobacco, rubber, and sugar plantations across Asia. St. Kitts had sugar plantations too! 🇰🇳
👆 Tap to reveal
Ecotourism
Touring NATURAL environments (rainforests, coral reefs, wetlands) in a responsible way that protects them and supports local communities. SE Asia, South Asia, and Caribbean are top ecotourism destinations.
👆 Tap to reveal
Delta
A flat, triangular-shaped landform where a river meets the sea, built up from soil deposits. VERY fertile farmland! The Nile Delta, Ganges-Brahmaputra Delta, and Mekong Delta are famous examples.
👆 Tap to reveal
Atoll
A small, ring-shaped island or chain of islands made of coral, surrounding a shallow lagoon. The Maldives (South Asia) is made entirely of atolls! Very vulnerable to rising sea levels. 🌊
👆 Tap to reveal

Our Physical World

🌍 Earth in Space — Rotation vs Revolution

🎭 Coryn spins in her chair — that's rotation! Then she walks around the teacher's desk — that's revolution! Same idea, just Earth doing it.
🔄 Rotation — Earth spinning on its AXIS (imaginary pole through the center, tilted at 23.5°). One rotation = 24 hours (1 day). Causes day and night.
🔁 Revolution — Earth orbiting AROUND the Sun. One revolution = 365.25 days (1 year). Causes our seasons. Every 4 years the 0.25 adds up to a Leap Year of 366 days.
🌐 Axis = the imaginary line through Earth's center from North Pole to South Pole, around which it rotates. Earth's axis is tilted at 23.5 degrees. This tilt is WHY different parts of Earth get more or less direct sunlight at different times — causing seasons!

☀️ Seasons, Solstices & Equinoxes

🎭 Adiaha's class is on a year-long field trip around the Sun. Their teacher marks 4 important dates on the calendar...
☀️Summer SolsticeJune 21Northern Hemisphere tilted TOWARD Sun. Longest day, shortest night. Sun at its highest point.
❄️Winter SolsticeDecember 21Northern Hemisphere tilted AWAY from Sun. Shortest day, longest night. Sun at its lowest point.
🌸Spring EquinoxMarch 21Neither pole tilted toward or away. Day and night EQUAL (~12 hrs each). Spring begins.
🍂Fall EquinoxSeptember 23Neither pole tilted. Day and night EQUAL again. Autumn begins.
💡 "SolSTICE" = Sun STICKS (stays long in summer, stays away in winter). "EQUInox" = EQUAL day and night.

🌋 Layers of the Earth (Outside → Inside)

1. Crust 🪨
Outermost, thinnest layer — where we live! Solid rock. Broken into 16 large tectonic plates. Includes mountains, valleys, and ocean floor.
2. Mantle 🌊
Thick, semi-solid flowing rock. Much hotter than crust. Its slow movement causes tectonic plates to shift, creating earthquakes and volcanoes.
3. Outer Core 🔴
LIQUID iron and nickel. Extremely hot. Its movement creates Earth's magnetic field, protecting us from harmful solar radiation.
4. Inner Core ⚫
Very CENTER of Earth. Scorching hot but SOLID because of intense pressure from above. Made of iron and nickel.
💡 Memory: "Can My Old Iguana Curl?" → Crust, Mantle, Outer core, Inner core

🧩 Tectonic Plates

Earth's crust is broken into 16 large puzzle pieces called tectonic plates. Heat from inside Earth makes them move slowly. There are 3 types of boundaries:

Convergent
Plates push TOWARD each other → mountains, deep trenches, volcanoes
Divergent
Plates move APART → rift valleys, mid-ocean ridges, new ocean floor
Transform
Plates SLIDE past each other → earthquakes, faults (San Andreas!)

🌐 Earth's Four Physical Systems

🌬️ Atmosphere
The layer of air surrounding Earth. Protects us from solar radiation and provides the oxygen we breathe. Examples: clouds, wind, weather, ozone layer.
💧 Hydrosphere
ALL of Earth's water — oceans, rivers, lakes, groundwater, glaciers, and ice caps. About 71% of Earth's surface is water, but only 3% is freshwater.
🪨 Lithosphere
All of Earth's solid land — the crust and upper mantle including mountains, deserts, valleys, and the ocean floor. Only about 29% of Earth's surface.
🌿 Biosphere
ALL living things — plants, animals, fungi, microbes, and humans. Supported by all three other systems working together.

⛰️ Key Landforms

Peninsula
Land surrounded by water on THREE sides, connected to mainland on one side. Example: Florida, South Korea.
Isthmus
A NARROW strip of land connecting two larger land masses with water on both sides. Example: Panama connects N. and S. America.
Island
Land completely surrounded by water on ALL sides. St. Kitts is an island! Japan, Taiwan, Sri Lanka too. 🇰🇳
Valley
A low area of land BETWEEN mountains or hills. Rivers often flow through valleys. Very good for farming.
Plateau
A flat area of land that is HIGHER than the surrounding land, with steep sides. Example: Plateau of Tibet (world's highest).
Cliff
A steep, vertical face of rock or earth, often at a coastline or canyon edge. Can drop hundreds of metres straight down.
Delta
A flat, triangle-shaped land at a river's MOUTH where it meets the sea, formed from deposited soil. Very fertile farmland.
Cave
A hollow underground space in rock or a cliff, formed by water erosion, volcanic activity, or wave action over thousands of years.

🏛️ Three Types of Government

Democracy 🗳️ — Citizens choose their leaders through voting. Advantage: People have a voice; decisions represent the majority. Disadvantage: Decision-making can be slow; majority can overlook minority needs.
Monarchy 👑 — A king, queen, or emperor rules, often by heredity (born into the role). Advantage: Stable leadership, quick decisions. Disadvantage: Citizens have little say; quality depends entirely on the ruler.
Communism / Dictatorship ✊ — One leader or party holds ALL power and controls the economy. Advantage: Can move fast, unified direction. Disadvantage: No personal freedoms, no free elections, citizens cannot protest.

🇰🇷 Korea — China's Cultural Influence

🎭 Jordan and Sydney visit Korea: "This feels very familiar..." That's because China shaped Korea's religion, writing, art, and government for centuries!
🛕 Religion: Buddhism spread from China to Korea in AD 300s and became Korea's dominant religion.
✍️ Writing: Chinese characters shaped Korean writing. Korean artists and writers used Chinese styles as inspiration.
🏛️ Government: Korean rulers adopted China's Confucian-based government — the idea that rulers should lead like wise, caring parents.

🗾 Japan — Islands, Shinto & Earthquakes

🎭 Andre, Markisio, and Miquea land in Japan. The ground wobbles. "Was that an earthquake?" "Yes," says the guide. "We get over 1,000 a year."
👥 Settlers: Japan was settled by TWO peoples — the Yayoi (mainland Asian farmers) and the Ainu (indigenous northern hunters).
📅 Calendar & Writing: Japan followed the Chinese calendar and adopted the Chinese writing system (later adapting it to Japanese).
⛩️ Shinto: Japan's native religion — belief that spirits (kami) live in ALL of nature: rivers, trees, mountains, wind. Teaches deep respect for the natural world.
🌋 Earthquakes & Tsunamis: Japan sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire — a zone where multiple tectonic plates collide. This causes 1,000+ earthquakes/year AND tsunami risk. Japan builds earthquake-resistant structures and has early warning systems. Imagine Coryn and Zalia trying to write an essay while the ground keeps shaking! 😱

🏭 China's Big Programs — Great Leap Forward & One-Child Policy

🏃 Great Leap Forward
Introduced by Mao Zedong (communist leader). Goal: rapidly increase China's industrial output — turn a farm country into an industrial giant FAST.

What happened: Regular farmers willingly left their fields and moved to factories. Two groups of intellectuals — teachers and doctors — were ORDERED to work on farms instead. Schools were shut down, students' education was disrupted badly.

Why it failed: No one was growing food → massive famine → millions died. The economy collapsed instead of booming.
👶 One-Child Policy (1979)
China's growing population strained the economy — not enough food, jobs, housing. In 1979 the government imposed: one family = ONE child.
Lasting effect: Children grew up as only children with total parental attention — called "little emperors."
Economy impact: Slowed growth, but later caused a shortage of young workers to support aging seniors.

📊 China vs Taiwan · Urbanization · Seniors

🏮 Mainland China
Communist economy. Rapid but uneven growth. Large gap between wealthy cities and poor rural areas.
🏝️ Taiwan
Free-market democracy. Became a tech powerhouse. Generally higher standard of living per person.
🏙️ Urbanization = city growth as rural people move in. Nearly half of China lives in cities. 83% of South Koreans are urban.
👴 Japan's senior citizens problem: Too few young workers are being born. This means not enough people paying taxes to support pension payments and elder care for the huge aging population. Japan is struggling to fund its retirement system.

🌶️ The Spice Trade — Europe Goes on a Quest

🎭 It's 1490. Luke, Andre, and Zamari are European merchants. Nutmeg costs more than gold. Pepper preserves meat for winter. "We MUST find where these spices come from!" So they sail...
🎯 What they searched for: (1) Spices — ginger, cinnamon, cloves, nutmeg, mace · (2) Wealth through controlling trade routes · (3) To spread Christianity
🏝️ The Spice Islands: The Moluccas and Banda Islands (part of present-day Indonesia). Portugal took Malacca in 1511 and discovered the source of cloves, nutmeg, and mace.
💰 Why such high prices? Europeans CONTROLLED the supply — spices grew only in specific islands they now controlled. Adiaha has the only juice box at school and can charge whatever she wants! 😄
🛳️ Two routes to SE Asia: Route 1 — Sail south around AFRICA then east (Portugal's route). Route 2 — Sail west across the Atlantic, then across the PACIFIC (Magellan's route to Philippines for Spain).
🇵🇹→🇳🇱 Portugal → Holland (Netherlands): Portugal funded its monarchy from spice wealth. Holland (renamed the Netherlands) found a new back-route to the Spice Islands in the early 1600s, joined the trade, and by mid-1600s (17th century) became the dominant trading power.

🏴 Colonial Rule, Resistance & Independence

🎭 Miquea, Zalia, and Shiloh imagine a stranger walking into their home, taking over, making rules, and telling them what language to speak. That's colonial rule. No wonder people resisted!
⚔️ Why resistance? Colonizers imposed their laws, religion, and language. They seized land for plantations, used locals as cheap labour, and gave people NO say in their own governance.
🇹🇭 One exception: Thailand was the ONLY country in SE Asia never colonized by Europeans.
1946 — Philippines 🇵🇭 (from USA)
1948 — Myanmar 🇲🇲 (from Britain)
1949 — Indonesia 🇮🇩 (Netherlands)
1950s — Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia (France)
1984 — Brunei 🇧🇳 (Britain)
2002 — East Timor 🇹🇱 — LAST!

🌾 Economy, Farming & Challenges

🌾 Most common livelihood = farming / agriculture. Most grown crop = rice. Most families practice subsistence farming.
💼 Why USA outsources here: Workers are paid much lower wages, letting US companies save money on manufacturing, call centres, and tech work.
⚠️ Why protecting the environment is hard: Poor countries need income from logging, mining, and farming NOW — even if it damages the environment long-term. Classic short-term vs long-term trade-off.
🌲 3 Environmental Challenges: (1) Deforestation — cutting rainforests for timber and farming · (2) Mining wastelands — large-scale tin mining destroys landscapes · (3) Habitat loss — endemic wildlife losing their homes
⚠️ Myanmar political challenge: Military coup in 1962 → decades of military rule, isolation, and poverty. Human rights abuses against minorities drew international condemnation.

South Asia

🔑 Key Vocab — Tap to Flip!

🌧️
Monsoon
tap to flip ↩
Seasonal wind that shifts direction and brings HEAVY RAIN for months. Coastal areas get 90+ inches/year. Fills rivers and irrigation systems — without monsoons, South Asia starves.
🌀
Cyclone
tap to flip ↩
A massive storm with violent winds and torrential rain — like a hurricane. Forms over the Bay of Bengal. Extremely dangerous to low-lying coastal areas like Bangladesh.
🔄
Reincarnation
tap to flip ↩
Hindu and Buddhist belief: after death, the soul is REBORN into a new body. How you live this life (karma) determines what you become next. Like a video game — die, respawn, new character!
🎯
Caste System
tap to flip ↩
A social system where you're BORN into a class and CANNOT change it. 4 levels: Priests → Warriors → Merchants → Laborers. "Untouchables" below all. India outlawed it in 1947.
💼
Outsourcing
tap to flip ↩
Hiring workers in OTHER countries to do work. US/Europe outsource to India because workers are English-speaking, highly educated, AND paid lower wages. India's tech economy exploded!
🌾
High-Yielding Crop
tap to flip ↩
A specially bred crop that produces far MORE food per plant than normal varieties. The Green Revolution introduced these to South Asia, dramatically increasing food production.

🌧️ Monsoons, Cyclones & Water

🎭 Vihan tells the class: "My grandparents wait ALL year for the monsoons." Sydney: "Wait — they WANT more rain?" Vihan: "Without it, there's no food."
🌧️ Monsoon → Farming
Rains flood rice paddies, fill irrigation canals, recharge groundwater. Without monsoons → crop failure → famine for hundreds of millions.
🌀 Cyclone dangers
Violent winds + storm surges (walls of ocean water) + flooding. Destroys homes, crops, roads. Bangladesh hit worst — flat and low-lying.
💧 3 reasons South Asians depend on water: (1) Irrigation for farming, (2) Drinking water for daily survival, (3) Transportation — rivers are highways. Why revered? The Ganges River is sacred in Hinduism — bathing in it is believed to purify the soul. Water = life + livelihood + spirituality all at once.

🏛️ The Caste System & Who Opposed It

🎭 Imagine Markisio, Zamari, and Kosi are sorted into permanent groups on Day 1 of school — forbidden to switch groups, marry across groups, or change their fate. Ever. That's the caste system.
1. Brahmins — Priests & Teachers (highest)
2. Kshatriyas — Warriors & Rulers
3. Vaishyas — Merchants & Traders
4. Shudras — Laborers & Peasants
❌ Untouchables (Dalits) — Below all castes. Forced into the dirtiest jobs. Treated as less than human.
3 negatives: (1) No social mobility — born poor, stay poor. (2) Untouchables faced brutal discrimination. (3) Divided society, prevented unity.
Who established it: The Aryans, who arrived from Central Asia around 1500 BC. They also created Sanskrit and wrote the Vedas. Who opposed it: Buddhism and Islam — both teach that all people are equal.

✊ Gandhi, Independence & Partition

🎭 Adiaha's class watches a documentary. On screen: a small man in simple white cloth leading millions peacefully. "He NEVER fired a gun," says the teacher, "but he toppled an empire."
🕊️ Mahatma Gandhi — led India's independence movement. Against British colonial rule. Used peaceful civil disobedience and boycotts of British goods. Worked with Nehru to win independence.
🗓️ India gained independence: August 1947 — after nearly 200 years under Britain.
✂️ Partition: India split into TWO countries — India (Hindu majority) and Pakistan (Muslim majority). Then East Pakistan broke away in the 1970s to become Bangladesh.
⚔️ India vs Pakistan conflict: Both claim the Kashmir mountain region. Multiple wars. Both have had nuclear weapons since the 1990s — making this one of the world's most dangerous disputes.

🌾 Green Revolution, Sanskrit & Outsourcing

📝 Sanskrit → ancient Aryan language → influenced Hindi (India) and Urdu (Pakistan). Like Latin influencing French and Spanish.
🌾 Green Revolution = program using high-yielding crop varieties, irrigation, and fertilizers to massively increase food production. India stopped importing food by the 1970s.
💻 Outsourcing: US and Europe hire Indian workers because they're (1) English-speaking, (2) highly educated, (3) paid far lower wages. Two environmental challenges of rapid population growth: (1) Air & water pollution from industry, (2) Deforestation — most of India's original forests are gone.

💧 Water: Hydropolitics, Dams, and Fossil Water

Dry region➜ Freshwater is scarce➜ Countries build dams➜ Downstream countries get less water➜ Tension grows
QuestionAnswer
Three uses of damsIrrigation, hydroelectric power, water storage / flood control.
Three countries with tension over major riversTurkey, Syria, Iraq.
Largest freshwater source in that conflictTigris and Euphrates Rivers.
How do Turkey’s dams affect Syria and Iraq?They reduce the amount of water flowing downstream.

Shortcut: Tigris + Euphrates flow through the story of Turkey ➜ Syria ➜ Iraq. If Turkey blocks too much water, Syria and Iraq feel it.

💰 Rich vs Poor Countries + Arab Spring

Rich countries
Qatar and UAE are often listed among the richest; Saudi Arabia is also very wealthy because of oil.
Poorest country
Yemen is commonly identified as the poorest in Southwest Asia.
Two challenges
Unequal development and political tension/instability.
Arab Spring
Protests beginning around 2010–2011 where citizens demanded change, jobs, freedoms, and better government.

Teacher-style “why” answers

If the question asks why oil dependency is dangerous, say: “Because the economy depends too much on one resource. If oil prices drop or oil runs out, the country can suffer.”

If the question asks why water causes conflict, say: “Because water is scarce, and upstream countries can control how much reaches downstream countries.”
